turns.response_html:
Nice find! At $25, that Motorola MC9090 CR (a specific configuration of the MC9090-G) is a classic piece of "tank-grade" enterprise hardware. Since it's from ISU Surplus, it was likely used for inventory in a warehouse or library on campus.

For a hardware enthusiast, this is a fun, albeit quirky, project device. Here’s the breakdown of what you’re looking at:

Technical Specs

  • CPU: Intel XScale PXA270 (624 MHz)—this was a beast for its time.
  • OS: Likely running Windows CE 5.0 or Windows Mobile 5.0.
  • Durability: It’s IP64 rated, meaning you can basically drop it on concrete or use it in a rainstorm without much worry.
  • Connectivity: 802.11a/b/g Wi-Fi and Bluetooth.

What Can You Actually Do With It?

While Windows CE is long-deprecated, there are still some cool hobbyist uses:

  • Terminal Powerhouse: If you’re into your custom terminal setups (like Fish or Neovim), you can use this as a dedicated, rugged SSH terminal for your Mac Mini or Raspberry Pi projects. The physical 53-key alpha-numeric keypad is great for CLI work once you map the keys.
  • Home Automation "Remote": With some effort, you can write simple apps (using .NET Compact Framework) to make it a dedicated controller for your Lutron switches or home server.
  • Retro Gaming: There are old emulators for Windows Mobile/CE that can run NES or GameBoy games. It’s not ergonomic for a platformer, but it’s a funny flex.
  • Parts for Robotics: If the software side is too dated, the laser scan engine and the high-quality trigger assembly are interesting components for hardware teardowns or custom droid builds.

Things to Check Before Buying

  • The Battery: These Li-Ion packs are likely shot if they’ve been sitting. Replacements are available online, but factor that into the cost.
  • The Screen: Check for "dead zones" on the resistive touch screen.
  • Charging: The tag says "Has Power / As is," and it’s sitting in a cradle. Make sure you get that cradle and the power brick, as they use proprietary connectors that are annoying to source separately.

At the price of a couple of pizzas, it's a great "ruggedized brick" to add to a tech collection!
